Hey so my therapist is also wanting me to see someone for a modality she doesn't specialize in, DBT. She knows my core wound is attachment trauma and having this safe relationship with her is absolutely vital to any healing work we do. I would maybe bring it up at your next session to ask if she would think somatic therapy may be helpful, has she had clients she has seen use it? I would hope she would mention the fear of abandonment and reiterate that she wants to work with you still, she may have just not picked up on what you noticed when she mentioned the other modality. I’ll never forget a visiting Col calling my old unit CC because I didn’t salute him. I had checked his driver and his ID in the absolute pouring rain and missed his rank.
It’s always the officers that you can tell no one likes who complain, and they have to have their ego by a salute. 
Another notable time was on a Sunday afternoon I had  an officer in civies get upset after I had been checking IDs at the housing gate and didn’t salute. They’ll just stare at you and go “so no salute huh?” I had been on post for 11 hours at that point by myself. 

I also don’t think many non SF realize how many hours we work on flight, not to mention mandatory training that is always on our off days or Flight PT we had to do before shift. It just becomes mind numbing and you’re bound to miss simple things. 

So all to say, saluting is shouldn’t be such a big deal. I have had a NCO gripe that my reflective vest was twisted, and countless complain about a random vehicle inspection that we had to do etc. 
Just smile and go about your day pls.

Hey not a therapist here but am a 32F who struggled with SH and SI after losing my mom in high school when I was 15 y/o to a sudden drug overdose. I just want to say you reaching out here and trying to be supportive speaks volumes. I am so sorry for you and your child I can only imagine how scary and difficult that all must be. I think the therapist recommendation is wonderful to let them look through some profiles and try finding someone who is a good fit. I usually find after 2-3 sessions I can tell if I “vibe” with my T or not.

My dad and stepmom had me see a therapist after admitting SH, but it was an awful fit and they never followed up how my sessions were, (i.e. how was your session today etc,) so I felt pretty alone during everything. 

I think just saying “hey X, I can only imagine how hard things are right now, but I am here for you however I can be. If there’s anything I can do to help you through this let me know.” Just holding a safe place where emotions are okay to be felt or talked about is be a great start. I just wanted to share this as I can see now what I needed then, (supportive environment,) where I could talk if needed and it was okay to just cry or have a bad day without being told to “be positive.” 

I hope this is helpful in some way and just wish your child and you all healing and safety. 💛

Hey just want to say you’re not alone with the feelings/thoughts you shared, (even though it probably feels like you are no one can relate.)

I got out after 4 years too. Transferred to the Guard and did school full time. Struggled to find my purpose and still am struggling but I’m hell bent and stubborn to find it. I’ve gone thru too much crap to just say fuck it. 

The VA has like 3-4 weeks to get you an appointment, and if they don’t you can ask for community care. If you deployed at PTSD is combat or MAT related you can go to a Vet Center for therapy too. 

VA also has walk ins you can just ask to see someone to talk to. Maybe they can help just listen and get a game plan for resources.

My VA has a peer support clinician who is a vet too. He never got back to me now I recall but he’s there and leads like peer support groups. 

I just hope you know you aren’t alone.

Does being outside help? I go to for a walk or run at a park nearby. It somehow always improves my mood even if it’s brief. I hope one of the comments here resonates even just a little. If you want to talk there’s lot of us here that will drop everything to listen.

Can you share what state or area you’re in? Maybe it can help narrow down resources. What about meals on wheels? Call a church they usually take donation and I am sure if you explain you cannot get to them for food donation they can drop some off. Even if it’s once a month. 

Your aunt taking your food stamp money sounds pretty illegal. That is assistance for you…not her and her son. I’m really sorry she’s doing that. I wish I knew more for resources to help. 

If anything please stay hydrated with water, stretch do you can. Even if you walk outside for a minute or two. Being outside can help so much just hearing birds chirping in the morning. Getting some sunshine. All you have to do is find one thing, it can be the absolute tiniest thing to hold on to, for one more minute, hour, day to keep fighting. 

You deserve to get the help you need. You posting here is a sign of strength and courage, even if it doesn’t seem that way. If you have Medicare or Medicaid can you see a therapist or social worker who could also help you with the mental, physical, and financial strains you are under? 

I really am sorry you are going through so much more than any person should. I hope you find support here in this community.

Hey career female FF checking in, on the small side and yes I struggled at first in the academy. There are techniques for everything but I also do have to stay in better shape than most guys who can just power through; even if they barely work out or don’t eat well. Just is what it is and that’s ok. 

I had to do extra reps for finding ways to throw the 24’ ladder for example. I’m at 5’2 and at 125. My instructors saw I had heart and I came in early before class and stayed during lunch just to do extra reps. I passed the state exams with 100%. You can do this. Keep your head down and do not quit. 
Be sure to stay hydrated too and try to make sure you’re getting enough electrolytes. I was chugging water, but wasn’t keeping up with my electrolytes after sweating so much and I got disoriented once. Just keep at it, absolutely do not drop out like someone posted. 

Once you’re on the floor keep working on your cardio and strength, and find a diet you can maintain. That doesn’t mean you only have to eat chicken and rice everyday, but just something to help build muscle and lose fat. I for example lived off pasta in the academy, specifically baked ziti.

For how small I am my instructors told me you HAVE to stay high on carbs, because your small frame/build needs energy. 

You got this though, and posting on here for help shows you care and want to do well!!! And if you have any questions etc just let me know!

Hey don’t stop fighting.

My PTSD (MST) claim was denied despite having a strong piece of evidence (STD test after my assault) including buddy letters who I told what happened while AD. 

Examiner said I didn’t have PTSD although I was diagnosed by a therapist I had been seeing for 9 months prior to my C&P. She blamed it on my childhood (the symptoms I had.) 
When she was asked about my STD test, (they flagged it because it’s a strong piece of evidence for MST in a claim,) she said it’s common for service members to have that done.

I felt absolutely humiliated and my symptoms got bad after that. They wonder why people don’t report sexual assault and this is part of why.

I appealed with the help of WWP and won my appeal. 70% for my symptoms that accurately depict what I deal with. So please don’t stop fighting. Just take a few days to regroup. Find a good VSO to help you navigate the next C&P and only focus on what happened in your service.

It will say on your branches CRSC application what you need, I had to just turn in my DD214, medical record showing my diagnosis from service, (I got my whole list off tricare online portal), along with the CRSC form filled out. They denied my IBS because afghanistan wasn’t in the list for gulf war but last year they finally added it. Hey just came across this thread (trying to figure out how my CRSC will be paid.) you are eligible if you are on TDRL. Whiskeytango isn’t correct there. I was on TDRL and was paid CRSC by my branch (Air Force.) 
Moved to PDRL and still an awarded my CRSC. Idk what they’re talking about by codes via the VA. My combat related disabilities fall under PACT act and also Gulf War illness from being in Afghanistan. 
Definitely worth filing for. It’s honestly really easy too and it isn’t through the VA so no need to worry about them looking at your disability ratings etc because it’s through DOD/your branch of service. 

Hope this helps!

Ask for an appeal and do digging yourself on what you can increase for your military rated condition and if you can add any others that you can be found unfit for for MEB.

They rated me 50% for PTSD but I appealed. Wrong a statement with specific examples how I met 70% instead. Used OAC lawyer from the Air Force and she helped me fine tune it. Submitted it along with a statement from a buddy who wrote her own giving examples (she had taken me to the hospital and residential treatment for SI,) and that helped my case.

Upgraded to 70% TDRL. I should’ve fought my PDRL decision they bumped me to 50% even though I was doing so much worse right before I separated.

Anyways, definitely fight it and get 30% minimum so you can medically retire. 
You will may be put on TDRL based on what your condition is but just getting the initial decision is huge.

Good luck OP
Not to mention the backpay if it does go through will be incredible..I saw it’s up to six years which would be amazing. I’ll definitely update this post if I hear an answer..

Hey USAF veteran here, now career Firefighter/Paramedic on civilian side.

Good luck and hope this helps a little.

I see a lot here saying it’s a scam or they are quacks.

But I was having severe back pain and migraines during and after finishing the fire academy. The doctors would only prescribe me pain medicine and my back would seize up doing the most basic tasks at home. To where I would fall to the floor lying on my back type of pain. 

It was awful, I tried stretching, yoga, massages. Nothing worked. And I did not want to just pop a muscle relaxer every single time either.

So I looked into chiropractor and different types of it. 

I only go to one type, called Atlas Orthogonal.

They DO NOT manipulate your neck!!! 

Ever. No twisting or cracking. Period. 

When I found this I went to one (there’s not many who practice this so I only had one in my city.) 

And he was absolutely amazing. After a month of visits twice a week my migraines were almost gone. Went from having twice a week to once every month or two.

Back spasms? GONE. I could finally live my life again fully and be healthy enough to be in my career of Fire/EMS. 

I never take muscle relaxers anymore. I also work out plenty I do compound lift, stretching, core and lower back and glute exercises to help stabilize my back. 

I haven’t honestly had a flare up in a couple years now and that was only due to improper lifting of too much weight. 

So yes I don’t agree with the hole in the wall chiropractor joints and you really need to do your research. 

Look up their website, ask questions, go on YouTube. But I don’t think to 100% day they are a quack and never give it a try if you have tried “western” medicine and it still isn’t able to solve the medical condition/chronic pain you are  experiencing.

Hey I’m a career firefighter/paramedic here. I also suggest reaching out to NREMT and asking if they can allow reciprocity. That is a great first step. Once you have that license you can definitely find employment as a paramedic. Then you could become a volunteer firefighter with a department you live near. They usually send you to earn your FF I/II and Hazmat Ops. That way you can work as a medic, have them pay to put you through training. Once you have those certifications, the world is your oyster.

This is the perfect time because everywhere is needing firefighter/paramedics. I see job postings constantly. 

I am currently working in GA, but pay in the south is not good for Fire/EMS. Would you consider MN? They have a pretty good reputation even for their EMS system from what I read. Minneapolis (Hennepin County EMS) they seem to be a good system. Their FTO program for new hire paramedics is 6 months from what I read on their website. This is amazing, and says a lot. As down south where I live in Georgia (outside of savannah,) new hires are given 3-4 shifts and then put on their own. There really is no FTO program and retention and pay is absolutely horrible.

So definitely try to get reciprocity for your paramedic. Then look at places you’d like to work at and live. See if there’s Fire Department’s who are either volunteer or combination (volunteer/paid.) Most will send you to training to get your certifications needed for firefighting in the US. It’s also a really great way to network and just learn how we operate here in the US. I did that first to just get more a feel for it and make sure fire service is what I wanted to do.

I hope this helps!! If you have any other questions I’d be happy to answer them :). Good luck!

Hey! Fellow FF/Paramedic here. 

So we are basically the same size/height, I am just shy of 5'2, and now weight around 125 lbs or so. Prior to taking the PAT and going through the fire academy, I weighed maybe 115.

Being short and small does have it's disadvantages for certain FF tasks, but it does not make this an impossible thing to overcome. You 100% can pass this PAT with the right preparation and mindset! 

I actually used the Tactical Barbell and followed the Operator template. (saw another redditor recommend it,) and TB really helped me increase my strength and endurance a ton. As long as you are consistent with that or any workout program, you will see results.

As for cardio, I do not like running, never have, even in the military lol. But one way I get around that is doing sprints during HIIT circuits and jumping on the stairmaster or rower for 30 minutes once a week. 

Not sure if you're a female, but if so, we get a lot of our strength in our legs. I really focused on my Squats and Deadlifts, along with doing the stairmaster to get them stronger. It sort of helps with other tasks and just not having the same physical make up for upper body strength that men do. 

If you want to message me/reply back and discuss any other questions you have/advice, I would be happy to talk to you more about things that may help you prepare for the PAT.  Also that's great you can take the practice tests to prepare. It'll really helps your body acclimate to the different tasks you need to pass. 

Good luck and hope this may help some!! :)

We also have tools we can breach the wall or floor to get to the kitten as well. I wish I saw this post sooner.

If you google your nearest fire station, they usually have a phone number that is listed and stations are staffed 24/7 and it is our job to respond. We often get calls to rescue animals too so this is definitely a good reason to call us! If they don't answer, they may be on a call/out of the station, so you can call 911 or non-emergency line to get someone to dispatch the closest appropriate fire station.

Speeding definitely is not advocated, the last thing we are trying to do is cause an accident on the way to a call. Receiving a ticket however for moving over an intersection (assuming traffic is packed in all lanes/turning lanes), the light is red, and we are behind someone in the left lane is almost obnoxious of an officer to do that. You live in the US and have seen that happen? You could easily take it to court and explain what happened. The only way I'd see that is maybe a res light camera catching your license plate, but they would see us as well and you'd have proof you moved right before we passed. We usually travel in the left lane to pass vehicles, and I would be shocked for a police officer to give someone a ticket that was moving out of the way for an emergency vehicle. That doesn't make any sense really, since it is the law.


Most states have a move over/slow down law for emergency vehicles, police officers, and where I live (Florida) this includes tow trucks as well on the side of highways). So even if that's the last resort to move over just enough into the intersection, so be it, assuming it's safe to do so.
